To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ethylene production and 1-aminocylopropane- 1- carboxylic acid-accumulation are important factors in the induction and development of plant tumours.

(1) Ethylene production is high in tumours and is regulated by the same factors as in normal plant tissue; and that (2) the host stem is affected by the tumour in such a way that its xylem is thickened, its rays remain unlignified and aerenchymatic tissue develops in the cortex.

ethylene is produced at high levels in plant tumors induced by the soil bacteria Agrobacterium and that this hormone is involved in the formation of aerenchymatic tissue, which allows the plant to breathe in its own stem.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of ethylene for the induction of tumour formation by Agrobacterium, the differentiation of the tumour tissue and the impact of ethylene on the surrounding host tissue and its physiology.
the question how a plant tumour is formed, and how it affects the physiology and structure of the plant.
the question of the role of ethylene in plant growth and development and in plant-pathogen interactions, especially in the context of the induction of plant tumours by Agrobacterium.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the tumour and host tissue produce ethylene and CO2 in response to the bacterial infection and the resulting tumour growth.
the tumour is a sink for ethylene, which is continuously produced in the tumour tissue, and that it has a strong impact on the host stem and cotyledons.
the tumour tissue is a highly active, metabolically and morphologically differentiated, but senescent tissue, and that the tumour is not a mere growth of undifferentiated cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the tumour and its surrounding host stem tissues are in a state of senescence and that this senescence is induced by A. tumefasciens.
A. tumefascens-induced tumours are a useful tool for studying the effects of ethylene on plants.

A. tumefasciens-induced stem tumours are characterized by high ethylene emission, which may be caused by an altered ACC metabolism, and that this ethylene is involved in the development of the tumour as well as in the adjacent host stem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ethylene produced by the plant tumour is not just a side effect but is a major component of the plant tumour phenotype.
A. tumefasciens-induced tumours are a unique model system to study ethylene production and its impact on plant growth.
the tumour is not a single, uniform tissue.
